question.problem: By the multiplicative property of congruences, ${15}^{4}≡$
question.worked_solution:
The multiplicative property of modular congruences states that if

$$
a≡b\,\text{and}\,c≡d\,(\text{mod}\,n),
$$

then, we have 

$$
ac≡bd\,(\text{mod}\,n).
$$

First, we decompose the exponent into a product of smaller exponents. For example,

$$
{15}^{4}=(3\cdot 5)^{4}={3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}.
$$

Next, we note the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{3}^{2} & ≡9\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\cdot 7+2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\cdot 0+2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\ {5}^{2} & ≡25\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡3\cdot 7+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡3\cdot 0+4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡4\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, by the multiplicative property of congruences, we have the following:

$$
\begin{aligned}{15}^{4} & ≡{3}^{2}\cdot {3}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\cdot {5}^{2}\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡2\cdot 2\cdot 4\cdot 4\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡64\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\cdot 7+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡9\cdot 0+1\, & (\text{mod}\,7) \\  & ≡1\, & (\text{mod}\,7)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that

$$
{15}^{4}≡1\,\,(\text{mod}\,7).
$$
